cells.tense: The fire is already moving in you and you are holding the pen.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're excited about, then take one small step toward it before the day ends.
cells.core:
Something's got its hand on your shoulder and it's your turn. People can feel the heat coming off you when you talk about what's next. Not the loud kind — the kind that makes someone else want to clear a chair for it.

That's your own learning energy arriving at the door. When it's going well you say the thing before you know where it lands. You start before every step is clear. Help and company show up because the confidence is genuine, and you don't need to name the ending first. The ask is small: pick the one thing you're excited about and move on it today. Keeping this is also a choice — feed it, or it goes quiet.
cells.sheetLine: The spark is here. Take it seriously and act on it.

cells.tense: You are bracing for a future you are already trying to write in full.
cells.ask: Before you start, ask someone one real question about it and listen all the way to the end.
cells.core:
You're outrunning this. Nobody's asked you to have the answer yet, but you're building the whole case in your head — the plan, the pitch, the part where they get it. The confidence is loud and it's mostly aimed at a day that hasn't arrived.

That happens when the spark gets taken for an answer instead of a spark. You're not wrong about the energy. You're ahead of it. The healthy version is the fire that learns first, talks after — confidence that can sit in a question without needing to close it. So leave the case at home for one conversation. Ask one person what they actually see. Stay quiet long enough to hear something you didn't already have.
cells.sheetLine: Confidence that won't sit in a question is a closing loop.

cells.tense: The door you were standing at has closed behind you and you have not moved.
cells.ask: Write down one idea you have been copying into the drawer and read it out loud to yourself once.
cells.core:
The spark is there, and you've kept it out of the room. Maybe it didn't get a chance to start, or someone stood on it and you stopped offering. So the light stays inward. You call it being realistic. You notice what other people build and think that's not yours to try.

What's quiet isn't inspiration. It's the learning energy holding its knees to its chest. Give it something small to grow on: write one idea down and read it back to yourself out loud. No audience needed. The confidence comes back the way anything living does — by being tended, not by being forced into a spotlight. Care that doesn't exhaust is allowed to include you.
cells.sheetLine: The spark isn't gone. It stopped being offered a place.

cells.tense: You are already opening doors and describing it as if you were only passing through.
cells.ask: Choose one thing you've been crediting to luck or timing, and say out loud that you built it.
cells.core:
Look at what started moving the moment you touched it. People follow your lead and copy your energy without you announcing it. You describe this as momentum, or the right moment, or somebody else's idea that worked out. But your hand is on it, and you haven't said so.

The spark has been operating without a claim. That's the failure here — not the fire, the silence about it. Writing the claim is a body thing: one sentence, said out loud, no rehearsal. No need to make it grand. Just let the builder own what the builder made, in the same breath with which you'd praise the person next to you. That kind of steadiness is what lets the shine hold.
cells.sheetLine: You built it. Start saying it out loud.

A reader could say the arriving thing is obligation or someone else's plan, and they'd be right to. The ask survives that: it still puts the spark in their hands as a decision, true either way.
